title: Where Can You Live in Florida and Avoid Hurricanes?
dek: No Florida beach town is hurricane proof. But Northeast Florida has taken far fewer direct hits than the rest of the coast, and where you live inside a town matters even more. Here is what 170 years of records show.
body:
No part of Florida avoids hurricanes, but Northeast Florida comes closest. From 1851 through 2018, NOAA counted 26 hurricane direct hits on the Northeast Florida coast and just one major hurricane, Category 3 or stronger. Northwest Florida, the Panhandle and Big Bend, took 66 hits and 14 majors over the same years.

Inland is safer than any beach town, because storm surge does the most damage and it stays near the water. If you want the coast anyway, the best move is a Northeast Florida town, on the mainland side, on high ground.

Which part of Florida gets hit the most?

Region (NOAA)Hurricane direct hits, 1851 to 2018Major hurricanes (Cat 3+)
Northwest (Panhandle and Big Bend)6614
Southwest4916 or 17
Southeast4916 or 17
Northeast261

NOAA's table splits the Southwest and Southeast major counts in a way that doesn't add up exactly, so we show both. The point stands either way: the Northeast has taken roughly a third as many hits as the Panhandle and a fraction of the major ones.

Recent years have followed the same pattern. Hurricane Michael came ashore near Mexico Beach in 2018 as a Category 5, and the Big Bend took Idalia in 2023 and Debby and Helene in 2024. Southwest Florida took Ian in 2022 and Milton in 2024.

Why Northeast Florida gets fewer direct hits

Geography is the usual explanation. The coast there bends in toward Georgia, so many Atlantic storms curve north and stay offshore, and storms that cross the state from the Gulf side have usually weakened over land by the time they reach it.

Fewer direct hits is not no damage. Matthew in 2016 and Irma in 2017 never made a direct landfall there, but both pushed water into downtown St. Augustine and flooded streets along the First Coast. Nor'easters in fall and winter also chew at the beaches.

The beach towns with the lowest hurricane exposure

These are the Northeast Florida towns we cover, with each town's score from our flood risk rankings (1 is the lowest risk, 10 the highest) and the typical home price from our town pages.

Notice the insurance column. The Northeast Florida coast has some of the lowest homeowners insurance averages of any beach county in the state, from the state Office of Insurance Regulation's July 2026 report. Insurers price for history, and the history here is quieter.

Where you live inside a town matters more than the town

Storm surge and flooding do most hurricane damage, and they follow elevation, not city limits. In our flood rankings, every one of the 15 riskiest towns sits on a barrier island or key. The safest five were all mainland or high ground towns:

  • Stuart, 1.5
  • Fort Walton Beach, 1.9
  • Melbourne, 2.1
  • Jupiter, 2.2
  • Palm Bay, 2.3

Those towns still get wind, and Fort Walton Beach is in the Panhandle, which gets hit the most. But a well built house on high ground in a region that gets hit often can come through a storm better than an older ground level house on an island in a region that rarely does.

How to lower your risk in any Florida town

  • Check the elevation and flood zone of the exact address, not just the town. FEMA's map service shows the zone; your county's GIS site usually shows elevation.
  • Look at the evacuation zone. Every coastal county publishes one. Zone A means you leave first and the water is most likely to reach you.
  • Buy newer or hardened. Homes built under Florida's stronger building code after 2002, with impact windows and a newer roof, ride out wind far better and cost less to insure.
  • Get the wind mitigation report and an insurance quote before your inspection period ends.

Our guide to what to check before you buy in hurricane season goes through each of these in more detail.

What about inland Florida?

If avoiding hurricanes is the top priority, inland North and Central Florida, around Gainesville, Ocala or the area north of Orlando, sees weaker winds and no surge. You give up the beach, and storms still bring wind, tornadoes and flooding rain. For a lot of families the answer is a mainland town 15 to 30 minutes from the sand, which keeps the beach in your weekend without putting the ocean in your living room.

Sources: NOAA Hurricane Research Division, direct hits by state and region, 1851 to 2018; Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Property Insurance Stability Report, July 2026; Florida Coastal flood risk rankings (FEMA flood zones and NOAA sea level rise data).
faq: What part of Florida gets the fewest hurricanes?
Northeast Florida. NOAA counted 26 hurricane direct hits there from 1851 to 2018, including one major hurricane, compared with 66 hits and 14 majors in the Panhandle and Big Bend.

Safer than most of the Florida coast, but not safe. Direct hits are rare, yet storms like Matthew in 2016 and Irma in 2017 still flooded parts of the First Coast. Elevation and flood zone matter for any address.
What is the safest Florida beach town from hurricanes?

No beach town is safe, but Northeast Florida towns like Daytona Beach, Fernandina Beach and Ormond Beach combine a quieter storm history with lower flood scores in our rankings. Mainland towns such as Stuart and Melbourne score lowest on flood risk.
Where in Florida has the most hurricanes?

Northwest Florida, the Panhandle and Big Bend, with 66 direct hits and 14 major hurricanes from 1851 to 2018 by NOAA's count, a total that includes Michael in 2018. Sally, Idalia, Debby and Helene have hit the region since.
